question: Which of the following is the best example of personal property (chattel) rather than real property?
choice_a: A refrigerator that is not built in and can be removed without damaging the structure
choice_b: A furnace permanently installed to heat the home
choice_c: Built-in kitchen cabinets attached to the wall studs
choice_d: Mature shade trees growing on the lot
explanation: Personal property, or chattel, is movable property not permanently attached to real estate. A free-standing refrigerator that is not built in remains personal property because it can be removed without damaging the structure, unlike built-in appliances, cabinets, or trees, which are generally classified as real property.

question: A tenant farmer plants and harvests a crop of corn each year on leased farmland. Under real estate law, these annually cultivated crops are classified as what type of property?
choice_a: Real property that automatically transfers with the land
choice_b: Emblements (fructus industriales), treated as personal property
choice_c: Fixtures because they are attached to the soil
choice_d: Trade fixtures owned by the landlord
explanation: Annually cultivated crops produced through labor and industry, called emblements or fructus industriales, are treated as personal property. A tenant farmer generally retains the right to harvest these crops even after a lease ends, unlike naturally occurring perennial growth such as trees, which is treated as real property.

question: A retailer leases commercial space and installs shelving and display cases to operate its business. Under the trade fixture rule, these items are considered:
choice_a: Real property that becomes the landlord's upon installation
choice_b: Fixtures that automatically convey with a sale of the building
choice_c: Personal property that the tenant may remove before the lease expires
choice_d: Emblements belonging to the property owner
explanation: Trade fixtures are items installed by a commercial tenant to conduct business and remain the tenant's personal property, even though they are attached to the real estate. The tenant has the right to remove them before the lease ends, provided any damage from removal is repaired.

question: When determining whether an item that was once personal property has become a fixture and part of the real property, which test do courts and appraisers most commonly apply?
choice_a: Whether the item was purchased before or after the property was listed for sale
choice_b: The dollar value of the item compared to the value of the real property
choice_c: Whether the item is mentioned by name in the property tax assessment
choice_d: The method of attachment, adaptation to the property's use, and the intention of the party who installed it
explanation: The classic fixture test examines the method of annexation (how firmly the item is attached), the adaptation of the item to the property's use, and the intention of the person who installed it. Courts weigh these factors together rather than relying on value or timing of purchase.

question: A deed in which the grantor makes the fullest set of covenants and guarantees clear title against defects arising both during and before the grantor's ownership is called a:
explanation: A general warranty deed provides the greatest protection to the grantee because the grantor warrants title against all defects, whether they arose before or during the grantor's period of ownership. A special warranty deed only covers the grantor's own period of ownership, and a quitclaim deed offers no warranties at all.

question: Which type of deed conveys only whatever interest, if any, the grantor currently holds, without any warranty of title or promise that the grantor actually owns the property?
explanation: A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the grantor has, with no covenants or warranties of title. It is commonly used to clear a cloud on title, such as removing a spouse's name after divorce, because it makes no promise the grantor actually holds good title.

question: For a deed to be legally valid and effective, which of the following elements is required?
choice_a: Recording with the county recorder's office at the time of signing
choice_b: Notarization by a licensed real estate broker
choice_c: A competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, and a legal description of the property, with the deed signed and delivered
choice_d: Consideration equal to the full fair market value of the property
explanation: Valid deed requirements generally include a competent grantor, a named and identifiable grantee, a legal description, words of conveyance, the grantor's signature, and delivery to and acceptance by the grantee. Recording is not required for validity between the parties, though it protects against later claims; nominal consideration is sufficient, and notarization is typically for recording purposes rather than validity itself.

question: A legal description that begins at a well-marked point of beginning and describes a parcel's boundaries using directions, distances, and monuments back to that starting point is known as the:
explanation: The metes and bounds method describes a parcel by starting at a point of beginning and tracing the boundary using compass directions (bearings) and distances (metes) between physical or artificial monuments (bounds), returning to the point of beginning. It is the oldest legal description method and is often used for irregularly shaped parcels.

question: A legal description that refers to a specific numbered parcel and block shown on a subdivision map recorded in the county land records is an example of the:
explanation: The lot and block method, also called the recorded plat method, identifies a parcel by its lot number, block number, and the name or reference of the recorded subdivision plat map filed with the county. This method is common for platted residential subdivisions.

question: Under the government (rectangular) survey system, the intersection of a principal meridian and a base line is used to establish grids of townships, each of which normally measures:
choice_a: One mile by one mile, containing one square mile
choice_b: Six miles by six miles, containing 36 square miles
choice_c: Three miles by three miles, containing nine square miles
choice_d: Ten miles by ten miles, containing 100 square miles
explanation: The government survey system uses principal meridians (north-south lines) and base lines (east-west lines) to create a grid. Each township is a square measuring six miles on each side, totaling 36 square miles, and is further divided into 36 numbered sections of one square mile (640 acres) each.

question: Under the government survey system, one section of land contains 640 acres. How many acres are in a quarter of a quarter section?
explanation: A section contains 640 acres. A quarter section is 640 divided by 4, or 160 acres. A quarter of a quarter section is 160 divided by 4, which equals 40 acres. This stepwise division is a standard land-measurement calculation tested on licensing exams.

question: A rectangular room measures 12 feet by 15 feet. How many square feet of flooring are needed to cover the room?
explanation: The area of a rectangle is found by multiplying length by width. Multiplying 12 feet by 15 feet gives 180 square feet, which is the amount of flooring material needed to cover the room.

question: One acre of land contains how many square feet?
explanation: One acre equals 43,560 square feet, a standard land-measurement conversion used throughout real estate for calculating lot sizes, density, and per-acre pricing.

question: A lien that attaches to all real and personal property owned by a debtor within a jurisdiction, rather than to one specific parcel, is best described as a:
explanation: A general lien attaches to all of a debtor's property, both real and personal, such as a judgment lien or an IRS tax lien. A specific lien, by contrast, attaches only to a particular piece of property, such as a mortgage lien or a mechanic's lien on the improved parcel.

question: A contractor who has not been paid for labor and materials used to improve a specific property may file which type of lien against that property?
explanation: A mechanic's lien is a specific, involuntary lien that a contractor, subcontractor, or supplier may place against the specific property they improved when they have not been paid for labor or materials furnished.

question: In general lien priority, how are property tax liens and special assessment liens typically treated compared to a previously recorded mortgage?
choice_a: They are subordinate to the mortgage because the mortgage was recorded first
choice_b: They are treated identically to judgment liens and rank by recording date
choice_c: They are eliminated automatically when the mortgage is recorded
choice_d: They generally take priority over the mortgage regardless of recording date
explanation: Real property tax liens and special assessment liens generally have superpriority status, meaning they take precedence over previously recorded mortgages and other liens regardless of when they were recorded. Most other liens, such as mortgages and judgments, rank in priority by their recording date under the rule of 'first in time, first in right.'

question: A nonpossessory right allowing a neighboring property owner to cross a portion of another's land to reach a public road, which continues to benefit the land regardless of who owns it, is an example of:
explanation: An easement appurtenant benefits a specific parcel of land (the dominant estate) and burdens another parcel (the servient estate), running with the land regardless of ownership changes. This differs from an easement in gross, which benefits a person or entity rather than a parcel of land, such as a utility company's easement.

question: A utility company holds the right to maintain power lines across a landowner's property, but this right benefits the utility company itself rather than any adjoining parcel of land. This is an example of:
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a specific person or company rather than a neighboring parcel of land. Utility easements are a common example, since the right benefits the utility company and does not require a dominant estate.

question: A landlocked parcel with no legal access to a public road may be granted access across a neighboring parcel through what type of easement, created by necessity rather than by written agreement?
explanation: An easement by necessity is implied by law when a parcel is landlocked and has no other reasonable access to a public road, typically arising when a larger tract is divided and one resulting parcel loses road access.

question: A person who has used a path across a neighbor's land openly, continuously, and without permission for the statutory period required by state law may acquire the right to continue using it through an easement created by:
explanation: An easement by prescription arises when someone uses another's land openly, notoriously, continuously, and without the owner's permission for a period of time set by state statute, similar in concept to adverse possession but resulting in a use right rather than title.

question: A homeowner gives a neighbor verbal permission to park a boat in the side yard for the summer. This type of permission, which can be revoked at any time and does not run with the land, is called a:
explanation: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use another's land for a specific purpose. Unlike an easement, a license does not create an interest in the land, does not run with the land, and can typically be revoked by the property owner at will.

question: A property owner builds a fence that extends two feet over the property line onto a neighbor's lot. This unauthorized physical intrusion is known as a(n):
explanation: An encroachment is an unauthorized physical intrusion of a structure, such as a fence, wall, or roof overhang, onto an adjoining owner's property. Encroachments can cloud title and often must be resolved before a sale can close, sometimes through a boundary line agreement or removal of the improvement.

question: An accurate survey is the primary tool used to detect which of the following potential title problems before closing?
choice_a: Unrecorded mortgages held by prior owners
choice_d: The marketability of the seller's credit history
explanation: A property survey shows the exact boundaries of a parcel along with the location of improvements, making it the standard tool for identifying encroachments and boundary discrepancies. Liens and other title defects are instead uncovered through a title search of the public records.

question: A deceased property owner's estate is undergoing court supervision to identify heirs, pay debts, and distribute assets, including real property. This court-supervised process that can affect title until completed is called:
explanation: Probate is the court-supervised legal process of administering a deceased person's estate, validating a will if one exists, paying debts, and distributing remaining assets, including real property, to heirs or beneficiaries. Property in probate can carry a cloud on title until the process concludes.

question: An existing lease on a property being sold is an example of a potential encumbrance because it:
choice_a: Gives the tenant possessory rights that generally survive the change in ownership
choice_b: Automatically terminates the moment the property is sold to a new owner
choice_c: Converts the tenant into a co-owner of the property
choice_d: Prevents the property from ever being sold while occupied
explanation: An existing lease encumbers title because it grants the tenant a possessory interest and right to occupy the property for the lease term; under the general rule, a sale does not terminate a valid lease, and the buyer typically takes subject to the tenant's rights.

question: A person who openly occupies another's land without permission, continuously and exclusively, under a claim of right for the period required by state statute, may eventually gain legal title through:
explanation: Adverse possession allows a person to acquire legal title to land by possessing it openly, notoriously, exclusively, continuously, and often hostilely (without the owner's permission) for a statutory period of time defined by state law. Until the statutory period is met and any required legal action is completed, it remains a potential encumbrance on the record owner's title.

question: The right to extract oil, gas, coal, or other resources located beneath the surface of a parcel of land is known as:
explanation: Mineral rights, also called subsurface rights, give the holder the right to extract minerals, oil, gas, and other resources beneath the surface. These rights can be severed from surface ownership and sold, leased, or retained separately from the rest of the property.

question: When a property owner sells or leases the mineral rights beneath a parcel while retaining ownership of the surface, this is an example of:
choice_b: A life estate pur autre vie
choice_d: Severance of a subsurface estate from the surface estate
explanation: Ownership of land can be divided into separate estates, such as the surface estate, subsurface (mineral) estate, and air rights. When an owner conveys the mineral rights while keeping the surface, the mineral estate is severed from the surface estate and can be owned, taxed, and transferred separately.

question: The right of a property owner to reasonable use and control of the space above their land, subject to public aviation and utility easements, is known as:
explanation: Air rights give a landowner the right to use and control the airspace above their property, which can be sold or leased separately (as is common with high-rise development), though these rights are subject to reasonable public and governmental use, such as aircraft overflight.

question: An owner of land bordering a river or stream generally has rights to reasonable use of the adjacent water, and in many states owns the land to the water's edge or the center of the waterway. These rights are known as:
explanation: Riparian rights belong to owners of land bordering a flowing waterway, such as a river or stream, and generally include reasonable use of the water and, in many jurisdictions, ownership to the water's edge or the thread (center) of the waterway. Littoral rights, by contrast, apply to land bordering non-flowing, larger bodies of water such as lakes, seas, or oceans.

question: An owner of property bordering a large lake or ocean, whose water rights extend to the high-water mark rather than to flowing water, holds what are known as:
explanation: Littoral rights apply to owners of land bordering large, navigable, non-flowing bodies of water such as oceans, seas, and lakes. These rights generally extend to the high-water mark, distinguishing them from riparian rights, which apply to owners along flowing waterways like rivers and streams.

question: In some western states, water rights are allocated under a system in which the first person to put water to beneficial use acquires a priority right to it, regardless of whether their land borders the water source. This system is called:
explanation: The prior appropriation doctrine, used mainly in arid western states, grants water rights based on who first puts the water to beneficial use, regardless of adjacency to the water source, following the principle of 'first in time, first in right.' This differs from the riparian doctrine, which ties water rights to ownership of land bordering the water.

question: When a single individual holds full and exclusive title to a property with no co-owners, this form of ownership is called:
explanation: Ownership in severalty, also called sole ownership, exists when title to a property is held by one individual or single legal entity, entirely separate from any other owner. The term reflects that the ownership is 'severed' from any co-ownership arrangement.

question: Two unrelated investors purchase a property together, each owning a 50% undivided interest that they can sell or will to whomever they choose, with no automatic right of survivorship between them. This form of co-ownership is:
explanation: Tenancy in common allows two or more owners to hold undivided interests in a property, which may be unequal in size, with each owner free to sell, transfer, or will their interest independently. There is no right of survivorship, so a deceased tenant in common's interest passes to their heirs or estate rather than to the surviving co-owners.

question: Three siblings take title to a property as joint tenants. When one sibling dies, what happens to that sibling's ownership interest?
choice_a: It passes according to the deceased sibling's will
choice_b: It passes to the deceased sibling's heirs under intestate succession
choice_c: It automatically passes to the surviving joint tenants by right of survivorship
choice_d: It is divided equally between the deceased sibling's estate and the surviving tenants
explanation: The defining feature of joint tenancy is the right of survivorship: when one joint tenant dies, their interest automatically passes to the surviving joint tenant or tenants, bypassing probate, a will, or intestate succession laws entirely.

question: To create a valid joint tenancy under common law, four unities must generally be present at the time the interest is created. These are unity of:
explanation: The four unities required for a valid joint tenancy are unity of time (interests acquired at the same time), title (interests acquired through the same deed or document), interest (equal shares and equal rights), and possession (equal right to possess the whole property). If any unity is broken later, such as one owner conveying their interest, the joint tenancy can be severed and convert to a tenancy in common.

question: A form of co-ownership available only to married couples in certain states, which includes right of survivorship and generally requires the consent of both spouses to convey or encumber the property, is known as:
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a special form of co-ownership recognized in some states, available exclusively to married couples. Like joint tenancy, it includes the right of survivorship, but it also offers additional protection because neither spouse can convey or encumber the property without the other's consent, and in many states it provides protection from the individual creditors of only one spouse.

question: A buyer purchases the right to use a specific unit at a resort property for one designated week each year, while other buyers hold rights to use the same unit during different weeks. This form of ownership is called:
explanation: A timeshare is a form of common-interest ownership in which multiple purchasers each hold rights to use a property, typically a resort unit, for a specific, recurring period of time, such as one week per year. Timeshares can be structured as fee ownership of the time interval or as a right-to-use arrangement.

question: In a condominium, an owner holds fee simple title to an individual unit along with what interest in the remaining building and grounds?
choice_a: A leasehold interest in the common elements that expires after a set term
choice_b: Shares of stock in a corporation that owns the entire building
choice_c: An undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the common elements, shared with all other unit owners
choice_d: No ownership interest in any area outside the individual unit
explanation: Condominium ownership combines fee simple title to an individual unit (typically the interior airspace) with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the common elements, such as hallways, roofs, elevators, and grounds, which is shared proportionally among all unit owners.

question: In a housing cooperative, a resident does not hold direct real property title to a specific unit. Instead, the resident owns:
choice_a: A tenancy-in-common interest in the specific unit occupied
choice_b: A life estate in the specific unit occupied
choice_c: A fee simple interest in the specific unit and an easement in the common areas
choice_d: Shares of stock in the cooperative corporation, along with a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit
explanation: In a cooperative, the corporation holds title to the entire building, and residents purchase shares of stock in that corporation. Ownership of shares entitles the shareholder to a proprietary lease, which grants the exclusive right to occupy a specific unit, distinguishing it from condominium ownership where the unit owner holds direct real property title.

question: Property held in trust involves a legal arrangement in which a trustee holds title for the benefit of another party. In this arrangement, the person who benefits from the trust's income or use of the property is called the:
explanation: In a trust arrangement, the trustor (or settlor/grantor) creates the trust and transfers property into it, the trustee holds legal title and manages the property according to the trust's terms, and the beneficiary is the person or entity who receives the benefit of the trust's income or property use.

question: A corporation that owns real property holds title as a single legal entity distinct from its individual shareholders. This means that upon the death of a shareholder, the corporation's real property:
choice_a: Automatically passes to the deceased shareholder's heirs
choice_b: Continues to be owned by the corporation, unaffected by the shareholder's death, since the corporation has perpetual existence
choice_c: Must be sold immediately and the proceeds distributed to shareholders
choice_d: Reverts to whichever shareholder has owned stock the longest
explanation: A corporation is a separate legal entity that can hold title to real property in its own name. Because a corporation generally has perpetual existence, the death of an individual shareholder does not affect the corporation's ownership of its real property; only the deceased shareholder's shares of stock pass to their heirs or estate.

question: A limited liability company (LLC) that purchases investment real estate offers its members what key advantage compared to holding title as general partners in a general partnership?
choice_a: Automatic right of survivorship among the members
choice_b: Exemption from all property taxes on the real estate owned
choice_c: Personal liability protection, shielding members' personal assets from the entity's debts and obligations
choice_d: A requirement that the property be sold within a fixed number of years
explanation: A key advantage of the LLC business structure is that it provides its members with limited personal liability for the entity's debts and obligations, similar to a corporation, while general partners in a general partnership remain personally liable for partnership debts.

question: A life estate grants an owner the right to use and possess property only for the duration of a specified person's lifetime. When the life tenant dies, the property automatically passes to a third party named in advance, called the:
explanation: When the creator of a life estate designates a specific third party to receive the property after the life tenant's death, that person is called the remainderman, and their future interest is called a remainder. If no remainderman is named and the property instead reverts back to the original grantor or their heirs, that future interest is called a reversion.

question: A life estate is created that lasts for the lifetime of a person other than the life tenant, such that the life estate ends when that other named individual dies, regardless of whether the life tenant is still alive. This is known as a life estate:
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie (French for 'for the life of another') is measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant. The life estate terminates upon the death of that measuring life, not necessarily upon the death of the life tenant occupying the property.

question: During the period a life estate is in effect, which of the following best describes the life tenant's rights and responsibilities regarding the property?
choice_a: The life tenant may sell the fee simple title outright without restriction
choice_b: The life tenant may use, possess, and derive income from the property but must avoid committing waste that would permanently damage the value of the future interest
choice_c: The life tenant has no obligation to maintain the property or pay property taxes
choice_d: The life tenant automatically becomes the remainderman upon reaching a certain age
explanation: A life tenant has the right to possess, use, and profit from the property during the life estate but is legally obligated not to commit waste, meaning they cannot take actions that would permanently reduce the value of the property to the detriment of the remainderman or reversioner. The life tenant generally cannot convey a fee simple interest since they only hold an interest limited to a lifetime.

question: A special type of life estate created by state statute that automatically gives a surviving spouse a limited interest in the deceased spouse's real property, regardless of what the deceased spouse's will states, is known as:
explanation: Dower (historically for a surviving wife) and curtesy (historically for a surviving husband) are statutory life estate interests that some states grant to protect a surviving spouse's rights in the deceased spouse's real property, regardless of the terms of a will. Many states have since replaced or modified these doctrines with elective share statutes, but the underlying legal concept of a statutory spousal life interest remains foundational.

question: When real property is transferred by a deed during the grantor's lifetime, this method of conveyance is referred to as:
explanation: Voluntary alienation is the transfer of title to real property by the owner's own free will, most commonly through the execution and delivery of a deed. Involuntary alienation, by contrast, describes transfers that occur without the owner's consent, such as through foreclosure, eminent domain, tax sale, or escheat.

question: A person dies owning real property with no valid will and no heirs who can be identified or located. Under the doctrine that prevents property from being ownerless, title to the property passes to:
choice_d: The federal government automatically in all cases
explanation: Escheat is the process by which property reverts to the state when an owner dies intestate (without a valid will) and leaves no ascertainable heirs. This doctrine ensures that real property never remains without an owner.

question: For a deed to effectively transfer title, in addition to being properly executed, it must also be:
choice_a: Recorded in the county land records within 24 hours of signing
choice_b: Delivered by the grantor and accepted by the grantee during the grantor's lifetime
choice_c: Signed by both the grantor and the grantee
choice_d: Witnessed by a licensed real estate broker
explanation: Delivery and acceptance are essential elements of a valid conveyance; title does not pass until the grantor delivers the deed with the intent to convey it and the grantee accepts it, and this must occur during the grantor's lifetime. Recording provides constructive notice to the public and protects the grantee's interest but is not required for the conveyance to be valid between the parties.
